title: A week of your rule
hook: look back at a week of living your rule
tomorrow: Shabbat comes with two commands, said in one breath. which two?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the broken tablets kept in the Ark: a righteous person falls seven times, and rises. Begin again. Now, with a week of the rule behind you, the honest look back.

A playlist you loved in spring turns into wallpaper by fall. Same songs, and you've stopped hearing them. Rules of life do that too. A line that felt alive on day one can turn into a box you tick. A sage in the Mishnah, Rabbi Eliezer, saw it happening to prayer and gave a warning that sounds almost like a contradiction. So do you change a rule that's gone flat, or keep it exactly as it is? The tradition argues both sides.
screen: `SPRING'S PLAYLIST, FALL'S WALLPAPER.` → `A LINE TURNS INTO A BOX YOU TICK.` → `CHANGE IT, OR KEEP IT?`

segments.voice: The argument turns on one word. Remember keva, from ten minutes of learning? Shammai, in Pirkei Avot: make your study keva, fixed. That's praise. But in Berakhot, Rabbi Eliezer uses the same word as a warning: whoever makes his prayer keva, his prayer is not tachanunim, real pleading. Same word, opposite verdict. View one says hold the line. A fixed time and a fixed text carry you through the dull weeks, and a rule you rewrite whenever it feels flat isn't a rule anymore. Its best case: the days you least feel it are the days the rule exists for. View two says watch for rot. The Talmud asks what Rabbi Eliezer meant by fixed, and gives more than one answer. One sage: prayer that feels like a burden. Another: prayer you can't add anything new to. Its best case: a rule that's become pure duty has stopped doing the thing it was for. Put them side by side and you get this week's line. Throwing the rule away loses what view one protects. Letting it go stiff loses what view two protects. So adjust: change the hour, shrink the size, add one new thing. Something to tell a friend tonight: the same Hebrew word for fixed is a compliment in one Mishnah and a warning in another.
screen: `KEVA: PRAISE IN PIRKEI AVOT.` · `KEVA: A WARNING IN BERAKHOT.` · `HOLD THE LINE, OR WATCH FOR ROT.` · `CHANGE THE HOUR, SHRINK THE SIZE.` · then, large: `ADJUST, DON'T ABANDON.`

segments.voice: Write your three-line rule from memory on a scrap of paper. Put a small mark beside the line that didn't happen this week. Don't cross it out: rewrite it underneath, sooner, smaller or simpler, so it fits the week you actually have.
screen: `THREE LINES, FROM MEMORY.` · `MARK THE ONE THAT DIDN'T HAPPEN.` · `REWRITE IT UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: A week of your rule: looking back honestly at seven days of living it, and tuning the line that isn't working instead of dropping the rule.
screen: `A WEEK OF YOUR RULE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: adjust, don't abandon. Same rule, one line rewritten for the life you've actually got.

screen: `DAY 1662 COUNTS.` → `A RULE OF LIFE · 15 OF 15.` → `TOMORROW: TWO SHABBAT COMMANDS, ONE BREATH. WHICH?`

howItsDone: Jewish prayer keeps a fixed text and fixed times, and the tradition also encourages adding personal words inside the fixed prayers; teachers of Musar and spiritual direction often suggest reviewing a personal rule weekly and adjusting it rather than dropping it.

match.prompt: one word, two verdicts — tap the pairs.

Rabbi Eliezer warns that a prayer made keva, fixed, is not real pleading.

so the cure is something new inside the old frame.
adjusting a rule means you've given up on it
adjust, don't abandon: rewrite the line, keep the rule.

fork.setup: your study partner wants to rewrite your shared reading plan every week to keep it fresh. you like it fixed. what's her side's best case?
options: a rule that never changes can turn into a burden; something new keeps it alive.
fixed plans are for beginners; serious learners improvise every day.
the Mishnah says a fixed study time is forbidden.
fork.reveal: that's the Berakhot side: prayer gone stiff, a burden, nothing new. your side has its best case too: the dull weeks are what the rule is for.

original.note: Hebrew: something new; a fresh thought added to an old text or practice.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rule is either kept perfectly or broken.
what it means: after a week, you tune the line that isn't working and keep the rule.
what a scholar hears: Mishnah Berakhot 4:4, Rabbi Eliezer's warning about keva, and Berakhot 29b's answers: prayer like a burden, prayer without pleading, prayer you can add nothing new to.
guess: looking back at seven days and tuning your rule
starting a brand-new rule at the end of each week
a week off from all your daily practices

chat.says: week one of my rule: the morning line never happens. always late for camp. drop it?
options: Adjust, don't abandon. Keep the line; change its hour or size so it fits camp.
Keep it exactly as written. Changing a rule means it was never really a rule.
Drop it. If a line feels like a burden, the tradition says it doesn't count.
chat.meaning: One view guards the fixed rule; the other warns it can go stiff. Rewriting the line, not dropping the rule, keeps both.

Rabbi Eliezer.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah who warned about fixed prayer

Berakhot.meaning: the tractate of the Mishnah and Talmud about prayer and blessings

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 1:15 (Shammai: make your Torah study fixed)
Mishnah Berakhot 4:4 (Rabbi Eliezer: one who makes his prayer fixed, his prayer is not supplication)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 29b (what is 'fixed': prayer like a burden; not said as supplication; one who cannot add something new to it)

notes: Berakhot 29b: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi in the name of Rabbi Oshaya (like a burden); the Rabbis (not in the language of supplication); Rabbah and Rav Yosef (cannot add something new). Two of these are given; names left out of the voice. Confirm.
The contrast of keva in Avot 1:15 and Berakhot 4:4 is a teaching device; a Keeper may note that the two passages use the word in different senses.
